title: ROI Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: ROI Calculator: Return on investment and annualised return. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and answers to common questions.
content:
The [ROI Calculator](/roi-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Return on investment and annualised return. Enter your amount invested, amount returned and investment length and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Return on investment (ROI) measures how much you gained relative to what you put in. The annualised figure lets you compare investments held for different lengths of time. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers. Related Finance tools include [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator), [Mortgage Calculator](/mortgage-calculator) and [Car Loan Calculator](/car-loan-calculator).

## How to use the ROI Calculator

Start by entering your amount invested, then entering your amount returned and finally entering your investment length (years). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. When you want a clean slate, Reset restores the defaults.

1. Enter your amount invested.
2. Enter your amount returned.
3. Enter your investment length (years).
4. Check the result — it updates instantly as you type.
5. Use Reset to start over with the default values.

## Formula

ROI = (Return − Investment) ÷ Investment × 100. Annualised = (Return ÷ Investment)^(1/years) − 1.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [ROI Calculator](/roi-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic. If the figures look wrong, check your inputs first — a misplaced decimal point is the usual culprit.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Investing 10,000 and getting back 14,500 after 3 years is a 45% ROI, or about 13.18% per year. Try the same figures in the [ROI Calculator](/roi-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves. The steps are the same whatever numbers you use; only the figures change.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Amount invested: 10000, Amount returned: 14500, Investment length: 3 years), the [ROI Calculator](/roi-calculator) returns ROI: 45%, Gain: 4,500, Annualised return: 13.19%. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. Change any value and every figure updates instantly. ## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Always compare annualised returns, not total ROI.
- Include fees and taxes for a realistic figure.

Keep these in mind and the figures will be as useful as the numbers you put in.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good ROI?

It depends on risk. Broad stock markets have historically returned around 7–10% a year before inflation. Try it with your own numbers in the [ROI Calculator](/roi-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Can ROI be negative?

Yes — a negative ROI means you lost money. Try it with your own numbers in the [ROI Calculator](/roi-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
